review.method: Assistant source-and-scope review; short original summaries of publisher pages
review.notes: Source checking is not cultural expert approval. Global dress codes retain publisher context; no universal batik-versus-handloom occasion ranking is asserted.

entries.title: Fibres used in Sri Lankan handloom textiles
entries.scope: EDB industry overview, not a fibre test or physical measurement of an individual sample
entries.text: EDB reports that most Sri Lankan handloom textiles use cotton and silk yarns. Handloom describes production, not a single fibre. Check the specific product record for composition, weight and drape.

entries.title: Sri Lankan handloom sarongs, shawls and sarees
entries.scope: Documented product forms, not permission for a particular ceremony or a gender restriction
entries.text: EDB lists sarees, shawls and sarongs among Sri Lankan handloom products, alongside household textiles. A sarong or shawl is a garment form; handloom identifies its production context. Ask hosts about event formality rather than treating a product listing as a dress code.

entries.title: Sri Lankan handloom cottage production and weaving heritage
entries.scope: Industry description, not proof of a photographed item's origin, handmade status or ethical certification
entries.text: EDB describes Sri Lankan handloom as largely cottage-based, with some larger manufacturers, and discusses preserving traditional weaving patterns. This supports a craft-context explanation, not automatic certification of every product sold as handloom.

entries.scope: Emily Post's Western etiquette examples; employer policy takes precedence, not a universal Sri Lankan office rule
entries.text: Emily Post treats business casual as variable: examples include slacks with a blouse, shirt or polo. Check the employer's policy.

entries.title: Plain weave construction
entries.scope: V&A textile glossary in historical embroidery context; not a photo classifier or GSM measurement
entries.text: V&A describes plain weave as alternating weft threads over and under successive warp threads. This identifies a construction pattern, not a particular fibre, weight or occasion.

entries.title: Satin weave versus silk fibre
entries.scope: V&A construction definition; the distinction from fibre is explanatory reasoning, not proof of an item's composition
entries.text: V&A describes satin using long warp floats that produce a smooth, lustrous surface. Satin is a weave term; it does not itself establish that a fabric is silk. Check composition separately.

entries.title: Velvet pile texture
entries.scope: V&A textile construction description, not a visual verification of composition or drape
entries.text: V&A explains velvet's raised pile through an additional warp system forming loops, often cut. Pile describes surface construction; it does not establish fibre composition or measured drapability.

entries.title: Garment care labels rather than fibre-only washing guesses
entries.scope: GINETEX system overview, not an item's care label, symbol recognition service or washing-temperature prescription
entries.text: GINETEX describes care labelling across washing, bleaching, drying, ironing and professional care. Professionals select treatments for their articles to avoid damage. Consult the particular garment's instructions rather than inventing a safe wash temperature from its predicted fabric category.

entries.title: Sri Lankan batik process and base fabrics
entries.scope: EDB industry account dated 2015; not a wedding dress rule or a measurement of a particular fabric
entries.text: Sri Lanka Export Development Board describes local batik artists using wax-resist decoration and dyeing. It reports batik clothing made in silk and cotton. Batik therefore describes a decorative process, not one fixed fibre composition. This account does not establish that batik is better than handloom for a wedding.

entries.title: Sri Lankan handloom sarees and textile products
entries.scope: Industry and craft description; not verified fibre, GSM, drape, environmental certification or universal occasion etiquette
entries.text: Sri Lanka Export Development Board identifies handloom textiles as a longstanding local craft. Its examples include handcrafted sarees, woven soft toys and upholstery fabrics, with varied designs, colours and patterns. The handloom label alone does not specify a garment's physical weight or a wedding dress code.

entries.title: Wedding invitation, ceremony and local custom
entries.scope: Emily Post etiquette framework; not a Sri Lankan religious or community-specific rule
entries.text: Emily Post's wedding guest guidance uses the invitation and time of the wedding to assess formality. It also considers the nature of the service, religious or cultural requirements and local custom. For a mixed-context wedding, clarify the invitation and ceremony rather than declaring one textile universally appropriate.

entries.title: Black tie wedding invitation
entries.scope: Emily Post's formal evening wedding guidance; not a universal Sri Lankan garment restriction
entries.text: In its formal evening wedding guidance, Emily Post lists a tuxedo as required when the invitation states black tie. This is a dress-code convention in that guidance, not evidence that a particular Sri Lankan textile or traditional garment is forbidden; clarify the hosts' expectations for traditional alternatives.

entries.title: Temple of the Tooth visitor clothing
entries.scope: Site-specific visitor guidance, not all ceremonies or Sri Lankan communities
entries.text: Sri Lanka Tourism's visitor description for the Temple of the Tooth advises covering shoulders and below the knees. Confirm the venue's current requirements; this does not establish a universal wedding dress code.

entries.title: Sri Lankan textile crafts
entries.scope: Craft context, not occasion-suitability ranking
entries.text: Sri Lanka Tourism lists batik and handloom textiles among local crafts. Their presence in this craft guidance does not show that either is always preferable for weddings, office wear or festivals.

entries.title: Batik is a production technique
entries.scope: UNESCO describes Indonesian batik; do not transfer Indonesian symbolism to Sri Lankan dress rules
entries.text: UNESCO describes Indonesian batik as wax-resist dyeing, including repeated dyeing stages. This is technique evidence, not proof of fibre composition or a universal occasion ranking.

entries.title: Sari and cultural context
entries.scope: Indian textile context, not Sri Lankan Osariya-specific etiquette
entries.text: The Victoria and Albert Museum describes the sari as an unstitched draped garment in its Indian-textiles discussion. That broad description does not determine which Sri Lankan drape, blouse or event dress code is appropriate.

entries.title: Component 2 recommendation explanations
entries.scope: Implementation facts; proposed cultural guidance is not expert-validated etiquette
entries.text: Component 2 ranks garments using recorded budget, occasion, weather, colour, style and garment preferences. Scores are rule points. Its optional Sri Lankan cultural bonuses are proposed hypotheses requiring expert review, not universal cultural restrictions. Explanation needs an actual supplied recommendation result.

entries.title: Component 3 fabric-to-design reasoning
entries.scope: Current prototype rules, not validated tailoring advice
entries.text: Component 3 uses recorded drapability and weight band for design ranking. GSM and stretch are context only. Category predictions do not verify composition or physical properties. Typical profiles are illustrative variants, not measurements of an uploaded photo. Ease ranges are provisional; explanations need the actual supplied design result.
